claim: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) prevents neurotoxins from entering the central nervous system.
source: Blood–brain barrier (BBB) prevents neurotoxins from entering central nervous system.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established knowledge about BBB function.

claim: Co-culture of SH-SY5Y and U251 cells markedly enhanced claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression in hCMEC/D3 cells.
source: Co-culture of SH-SY5Y and U251 cells markedly enhanced claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression in hCMEC/D3 cells, accompanied by increased transendothelial electrical resistance and decreased permeability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing increased protein expression in co-culture conditions.

claim: Co-culture of SH-SY5Y and U251 cells with hCMEC/D3 cells increased transendothelial electrical resistance.
source: Co-culture of SH-SY5Y and U251 cells markedly enhanced claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression in hCMEC/D3 cells, accompanied by increased transendothelial electrical resistance and decreased permeability.
evidence: This is supported by TEER measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Co-culture of SH-SY5Y and U251 cells with hCMEC/D3 cells decreased permeability.
source: Co-culture of SH-SY5Y and U251 cells markedly enhanced claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression in hCMEC/D3 cells, accompanied by increased transendothelial electrical resistance and decreased permeability.
evidence: This is supported by permeability measurements shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Conditioned medium from SH-SY5Y cells promoted claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression.
source: Conditioned medium (CM) from SH-SY5Y cells (S-CM), U251 cells (U-CM), and co-culture of SH-SY5Y and U251 cells (US-CM) also promoted claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Conditioned medium from U251 cells promoted claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression.
source: Conditioned medium (CM) from SH-SY5Y cells (S-CM), U251 cells (U-CM), and co-culture of SH-SY5Y and U251 cells (US-CM) also promoted claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Conditioned medium from co-culture of SH-SY5Y and U251 cells promoted claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression.
source: Conditioned medium (CM) from SH-SY5Y cells (S-CM), U251 cells (U-CM), and co-culture of SH-SY5Y and U251 cells (US-CM) also promoted claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GDNF levels in S-CM and US-CM were significantly higher than CMs from hCMEC/D3 and U-CM.
source: Glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) levels in S-CM and US-CM were significantly higher than CMs from hCMEC/D3 and U-CM.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: GDNF upregulated claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression.
source: Both GDNF and US-CM upregulated claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression, which were attenuated by anti-GDNF antibody and GDNF signaling inhibitors.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: US-CM upregulated claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression.
source: Both GDNF and US-CM upregulated claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression, which were attenuated by anti-GDNF antibody and GDNF signaling inhibitors.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Anti-GDNF antibody attenuated GDNF-induced upregulation of claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression.
source: Both GDNF and US-CM upregulated claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression, which were attenuated by anti-GDNF antibody and GDNF signaling inhibitors.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2H and 2I.

claim: GDNF signaling inhibitors attenuated GDNF-induced upregulation of claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression.
source: Both GDNF and US-CM upregulated claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression, which were attenuated by anti-GDNF antibody and GDNF signaling inhibitors.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2K and 2L.

claim: GDNF increased claudin-5 expression via the PI3K/AKT/FOXO1 pathway.
source: GDNF increased claudin-5 expression via the PI3K/AKT/FOXO1 and MAPK/ERK pathways.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing pathway activation and inhibitor studies in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: GDNF increased claudin-5 expression via the MAPK/ERK pathway.
source: GDNF increased claudin-5 expression via the PI3K/AKT/FOXO1 and MAPK/ERK pathways.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing pathway activation and inhibitor studies in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: GDNF promoted VE-cadherin expression by activating PI3K/AKT/ETS1 signaling.
source: Meanwhile, GDNF promoted VE-cadherin expression by activating PI3K/AKT/ETS1 and MAPK/ERK/ETS1 signaling.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing pathway activation and ETS1 knockdown studies in Figure 5.

claim: GDNF promoted VE-cadherin expression by activating MAPK/ERK/ETS1 signaling.
source: Meanwhile, GDNF promoted VE-cadherin expression by activating PI3K/AKT/ETS1 and MAPK/ERK/ETS1 signaling.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing pathway activation and ETS1 knockdown studies in Figure 5.

claim: The roles of GDNF in BBB integrity were validated using brain-specific Gdnf silencing mice.
source: The roles of GDNF in BBB integrity were validated using brain-specific Gdnf silencing mice.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The developed triple co-culture BBB model was successfully applied to predict BBB permeability.
source: The developed triple co-culture BBB model was successfully applied to predict BBB permeability.
evidence: This is supported by permeability prediction data for 18 drugs shown in Figure 7 and Table 1.

claim: Neurons enhance BBB integrity by upregulating claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression through GDNF secretion.
source: In conclusion, neurons enhance BBB integrity by upregulating claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression through GDNF secretion and established triple co-culture BBB model may be used to predict drugs' BBB permeability.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: The established triple co-culture BBB model may be used to predict drugs' BBB permeability.
source: In conclusion, neurons enhance BBB integrity by upregulating claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression through GDNF secretion and established triple co-culture BBB model may be used to predict drugs' BBB permeability.
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro/in vivo correlation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: BBB maintains homeostasis and normal function of CNS by strictly regulating material exchange between the blood and brain.
source: As a dynamic interface between the blood circulatory system and the central nervous system (CNS), the blood–brain barrier (BBB) maintains homeostasis and normal function of CNS by strictly regulating material exchange between the blood and brain (Palmiotti et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about BBB function supported by citation.

claim: The maintenance of BBB is mainly attributed to the expression of tight junctions and adherent junctions between adjacent brain endothelial cells and a variety of drug transporters.
source: The maintenance of BBB is mainly attributed to the expression of tight junctions (TJ) and adherent junctions (AJ) between adjacent brain endothelial cells and a variety of drug transporters.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BBB structure and function.

claim: BBB restricts the transport of some drugs from blood to brain, leading to poor CNS therapeutic effects and even CNS treatment failure.
source: However, as a double-edged sword that protects CNS function, BBB also restricts the transport of some drugs from blood to brain, leading to poor CNS therapeutic effects and even CNS treatment failure (Banks, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The in situ brain perfusion (ISBP) is considered the 'gold standard' for assessing BBB permeability.
source: The in situ brain perfusion (ISBP) is considered the 'gold standard' for assessing BBB permeability but there exist limits related to animal ethics.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: ISBP has limits related to animal ethics.
source: The in situ brain perfusion (ISBP) is considered the 'gold standard' for assessing BBB permeability but there exist limits related to animal ethics.
evidence: This is a known limitation of the ISBP method.

claim: ISBP is not suitable for human or high-throughput workflows.
source: Moreover, ISBP is not suitable for human or high-throughput workflows.
evidence: This is a known limitation of the ISBP method.

claim: BBB is formed by neurovascular units (NVU), composed of neural (neurons, microglia, and astrocytes) and vascular components (vascular endothelial cells, pericytes, and vascular smooth muscle cells).
source: BBB is formed by neurovascular units (NVU), composed of neural (neurons, microglia, and astrocytes) and vascular components (vascular endothelial cells, pericytes, and vascular smooth muscle cells) (Potjewyd et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about BBB structure supported by citation.

claim: The constant crosstalk and interactions among NVU cells contribute to the structural and signaling-based regulation of transcellular and paracellular transport, control of BBB permeability, and regulation of cerebral circulation.
source: The constant crosstalk and interactions among these cells contribute to the structural and signaling-based regulation of transcellular and paracellular transport, control of BBB permeability, and regulation of cerebral circulation (Arvanitis et al., 2020; Muoio et al., 2014; Potjewyd et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In vitro mono-culture of BMECs tends to lose some unique characteristics without the support of other cell types.
source: Although brain microvascular endothelial cells (BMECs) are commonly utilized as an in vitro BBB model to assess drug permeability across BBB, in vitro mono-culture of BMECs tends to lose some unique characteristics without the support of other cell types.
evidence: This is established knowledge about limitations of mono-culture BBB models.

claim: Astrocytes are the most abundant glial cell type in brain.
source: Astrocytes are the most abundant glial cell type in brain (Clasadonte and Prevot, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Astrocyte terminal feet cover >80% of the surface of capillaries to form interdigitating coverage without slits.
source: Their terminal feet cover >80% of the surface of capillaries to form interdigitating coverage without slits (Mathiisen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about astrocyte anatomy supported by citation.

claim: The maturation of BBB in mice considerably overlaps with the establishment of neuronal activity.
source: The maturation of BBB in mice considerably overlaps with the establishment of neuronal activity (Biswas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The conditioned medium collected from primary rat neurons attenuated cell death caused by glucose–oxygen–serum deprivation.
source: A study revealed that the conditioned medium (CM) collected from primary rat neurons also attenuated cell death caused by glucose–oxygen–serum deprivation (Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: Primary rat neurons were reported to affect the differentiation and formation of BMECs.
source: Furthermore, the primary rat neurons were reported to affect the differentiation and formation of BMECs (Savettieri et al., 2000; Schiera et al., 2003; Xue et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Triple co-culture of hCMEC/D3, 1321N1, and SH-SY5Y cells exhibited a higher TEER compared with the double co-culture of hCMEC/D3 and 1321N1.
source: Recent research reported that, compared with the double co-culture of hCMEC/D3 and 1321N1 (human astrocytoma cells), the triple co-culture of hCMEC/D3, 1321N1, and human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells exhibited a higher transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Barberio et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: Co-cultivation of RBE4.B and neurons resulted in lower permeability of [3H] sucrose than RBE4.B cells grown alone.
source: A similar report showed that co-cultivation of RBE4.B (rat brain capillary endothelial cells) and neurons resulted in the lower permeability of [3H] sucrose than RBE4.B cells grown alone (Schiera et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: TEER values of the four in vitro BBB models gradually increased until day 6.
source: TEER values were measured during the co-culture (Figure 1B). TEER values of the four in vitro BBB models gradually increased until day 6.
evidence: This is supported by TEER measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: On day 7, the TEER values showed a decreasing trend.
source: On day 7, the TEER values showed a decreasing trend.
evidence: This is an observation from the TEER measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The highest TEER values were observed in the triple co-culture BBB model.
source: The highest TEER values were observed in the triple co-culture BBB model, followed by double co-culture with U251 cells and double co-culture with SH-SY5Y cells BBB models, hCMEC/D3 cells mono-culture BBB model showed the lowest TEER values.
evidence: This is supported by TEER measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: U251 cells themselves contributed to the physical barrier of the model.
source: We also measured the TEER values of U251 monolayer cells, and the results showed that U251 cells themselves also contributed to the physical barrier of the model (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by TEER measurements of U251 monolayer shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The triple co-culture BBB model showed the lowest permeability of fluorescein and FITC-Dex.
source: Consistent with the TEER values, the triple co-culture BBB model showed the lowest permeability of fluorescein and FITC-Dex, followed by double co-culture with U251 cells and double co-culture with SH-SY5Y cells BBB models.
evidence: This is supported by permeability measurements shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Monolayer of U251 cells itself worked as a barrier, preventing the leakage of permeability markers.
source: It was noticed that monolayer of U251 cells itself also worked as a barrier, preventing the leakage of permeability markers, which may explain why the permeability of FITC-Dex in double co-culture model with U251 cells is lower than that in double co-culture model with SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by permeability measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Co-culture with SH-SY5Y, U251, and U251 + SH-SY5Y cells enhanced the proliferation of hCMEC/D3 cells.
source: Co-culture with SH-SY5Y, U251, and U251 + SH-SY5Y cells also enhanced the proliferation of hCMEC/D3 cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell density, EdU incorporation, and cell viability data shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: The promoting effect of SH-SY5Y cells on hCMEC/D3 proliferation was stronger than that of U251 cells.
source: Moreover, the promoting effect of SH-SY5Y cells was stronger than that of U251 cells (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: Incubation with bFGF increased cell proliferation and reduced permeabilities of fluorescein and FITC-Dex across hCMEC/D3 cell monolayer.
source: The results showed that incubation with bFGF increased cell proliferation and reduced permeabilities of fluorescein and FITC-Dex across hCMEC/D3 cell monolayer.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The permeability reduction by bFGF was less than that by double co-culture with U251 cells or triple co-culture.
source: However, the permeability reduction was less than that by double co-culture with U251 cells or triple co-culture.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 with other figures.

claim: Contribution of cell proliferation to the barrier function of hCMEC/D3 was minor.
source: These results inferred that contribution of cell proliferation to the barrier function of hCMEC/D3 was minor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the bFGF experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Double co-culture with SH-SY5Y, double co-culture with U251, and triple co-culture BBB models showed markedly increases in claudin-5, VE-cadherin, β-catenin, and BCRP mRNA expression compared with hCMEC/D3 cell mono-culture model.
source: Compared with hCMEC/D3 cell mono-culture model, double co-culture with SH-SY5Y, double co-culture with U251, and triple co-culture BBB models showed markedly increases in claudin-5, VE-cadherin, β-catenin, and BCRP mRNA expression.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1J and 1K.

claim: Notably increased claudin-5 expression was detected in double co-culture with SH-SY5Y cells and triple co-culture BBB models.
source: Notably increased claudin-5 expression was detected in double co-culture with SH-SY5Y cells and triple co-culture BBB models, while VE-cadherin expression was markedly increased in double co-culture with U251 cells and triple co-culture BBB models.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1L-O.

claim: VE-cadherin expression was markedly increased in double co-culture with U251 cells and triple co-culture BBB models.
source: Notably increased claudin-5 expression was detected in double co-culture with SH-SY5Y cells and triple co-culture BBB models, while VE-cadherin expression was markedly increased in double co-culture with U251 cells and triple co-culture BBB models.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1L-O.

claim: Expression levels of ZO-1 and occludin were unaltered by co-culture.
source: Expression levels of other TJ proteins (ZO-1 and occludin) and AJ protein (β-catenin) were unaltered.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1L-O.

claim: Expression of BCRP was slightly affected by co-cultivation with U251 cells.
source: The expression of BCRP was slightly affected by co-cultivation with U251 cells.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1N-O.

claim: Significant negative correlations were found between Papp values of fluorescein and the expression of claudin-5.
source: Significant negative correlations were found between Papp values of fluorescein and the expression of claudin-5 or VE-cadherin.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1P.

claim: Significant negative correlations were found between Papp values of fluorescein and the expression of VE-cadherin.
source: Significant negative correlations were found between Papp values of fluorescein and the expression of claudin-5 or VE-cadherin.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1Q.

claim: Papp values of FITC-Dex were negatively correlated to the expression levels of claudin-5.
source: Papp values of FITC-Dex were also negatively correlated to the expression levels of claudin-5 or VE-cadherin (Figure 1P–S).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1R.

claim: Papp values of FITC-Dex were negatively correlated to the expression levels of VE-cadherin.
source: Papp values of FITC-Dex were also negatively correlated to the expression levels of claudin-5 or VE-cadherin (Figure 1P–S).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1S.

claim: The decreased permeability of fluorescein and FITC-Dex mainly results from the upregulated expression of both claudin-5 and VE-cadherin.
source: These results indicate that the decreased permeability of fluorescein and FITC-Dex mainly results from the upregulated expression of both claudin-5 and VE-cadherin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation data shown in Figure 1P-S.

claim: Both S-CM, U-CM, and US-CM markedly increased the expression of claudin-5 and VE-cadherin.
source: Both S-CM, U-CM, and US-CM markedly increased the expression of claudin-5 and VE-cadherin.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: US-CM showed the strongest induction effects on claudin-5 and VE-cadherin.
source: US-CM showed the strongest induction effects on claudin-5 and VE-cadherin.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: U251 or SH-SY5Y cells exhibited significantly higher expression levels of GDNF, nerve growth factor, IGF-1, vascular endothelial growth factor, bFGF, and TGF-β compared to hCMEC/D3 cells.
source: The results showed that U251 or SH-SY5Y cells exhibited significantly higher expression levels of glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), nerve growth factor, insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), vascular endothelial growth factor, bFGF, and transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) compared to hCMEC/D3 cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The mRNA expression of GDNF, IGF-1, TGF-β, and bFGF in SH-SY5Y cells was higher than those in U251 cells.
source: Furthermore, the mRNA expression of GDNF, IGF-1, TGF-β, and bFGF in SH-SY5Y cells was higher than those in U251 cells.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GDNF has been reported to promote BBB integrity.
source: In these cytokines, GDNF (Dong and Ubogu, 2018; Igarashi et al., 1999; Shimizu et al., 2012), bFGF (Shimizu et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2016), IGF-1 (Ko et al., 2009; Nowrangi et al., 2019), and TGF-β (Fu et al., 2021) have been reported to promote BBB integrity.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: bFGF has been reported to promote BBB integrity.
source: In these cytokines, GDNF (Dong and Ubogu, 2018; Igarashi et al., 1999; Shimizu et al., 2012), bFGF (Shimizu et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2016), IGF-1 (Ko et al., 2009; Nowrangi et al., 2019), and TGF-β (Fu et al., 2021) have been reported to promote BBB integrity.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: IGF-1 has been reported to promote BBB integrity.
source: In these cytokines, GDNF (Dong and Ubogu, 2018; Igarashi et al., 1999; Shimizu et al., 2012), bFGF (Shimizu et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2016), IGF-1 (Ko et al., 2009; Nowrangi et al., 2019), and TGF-β (Fu et al., 2021) have been reported to promote BBB integrity.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: TGF-β has been reported to promote BBB integrity.
source: In these cytokines, GDNF (Dong and Ubogu, 2018; Igarashi et al., 1999; Shimizu et al., 2012), bFGF (Shimizu et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2016), IGF-1 (Ko et al., 2009; Nowrangi et al., 2019), and TGF-β (Fu et al., 2021) have been reported to promote BBB integrity.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Levels of GDNF, bFGF, and IGF-1 in S-CM and US-CM were significantly higher than CMs from hCMEC/D3 cells and U-CM.
source: The results showed that levels of GDNF, bFGF, and IGF-1 in S-CM and US-CM were significantly higher than CMs from hCMEC/D3 cells (H-CM) and U-CM, but levels of TGF-β in S-CM and U-CM were lower than those in H-CM.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Levels of TGF-β in S-CM and U-CM were lower than those in H-CM.
source: The results showed that levels of GDNF, bFGF, and IGF-1 in S-CM and US-CM were significantly higher than CMs from hCMEC/D3 cells (H-CM) and U-CM, but levels of TGF-β in S-CM and U-CM were lower than those in H-CM.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The level of IGF-1 in US-CM was remarkably lower than that in S-CM.
source: Interestingly, the level of IGF-1 in US-CM was remarkably lower than that in S-CM, indicating that U251 cells suppressed IGF-1 secretion from SH-SY5Y.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: U251 cells suppressed IGF-1 secretion from SH-SY5Y.
source: Interestingly, the level of IGF-1 in US-CM was remarkably lower than that in S-CM, indicating that U251 cells suppressed IGF-1 secretion from SH-SY5Y.
evidence: This is an inference based on the IGF-1 measurement data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Only GDNF induced the expression of claudin-5 and VE-cadherin in a concentration-dependent manner among the four tested neurotrophic factors.
source: Among the four tested neurotrophic factors, only GDNF induced the expression of claudin-5 and VE-cadherin in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D-G.

claim: A high level (5 ng/ml) of TGF-β slightly downregulated claudin-5 expression.
source: In contrast, a high level (5 ng/ml) of TGF-β slightly downregulated claudin-5 expression (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Upregulation of claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression by US-CM are attributed to secreted GDNF.
source: These results demonstrate that upregulation of claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression by US-CM are attributed to secreted GDNF.
evidence: This is an inference based on the neurotrophic factor experiments shown in Figure 2D-G.

claim: The anti-GDNF antibody concentration-dependently reversed the US-CM-induced claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression.
source: Consistent with our expectation, the anti-GDNF antibody concentration-dependent reversed the US-CM-induced claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: GDNF-induced upregulation of claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression was reversed by the anti-GDNF antibody.
source: Furthermore, GDNF-induced upregulation of claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression was also reversed by the anti-GDNF antibody (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The induction effects of US-CM and GDNF on the claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression in hCMEC/D3 cells were confirmed in primary rat BMECs.
source: The induction effects of US-CM and GDNF on the claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression in hCMEC/D3 cells were also confirmed in primary rat BMECs (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: GDNF forms a heterohexameric complex with two GFRα1 molecules and two RET receptors to activate the GDNF–GFRα1–RET signaling.
source: GDNF forms a heterohexameric complex with two GFRα1 molecules and two RET receptors to activate the GDNF–GFRα1–RET signaling (Fielder et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GDNF signaling supported by citation.

claim: Both SPP-86 and PP2 markedly attenuated claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression induced by GDNF.
source: Both SPP-86 and PP2 markedly attenuated claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression induced by GDNF (Figure 2K) and US-CM (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Both SPP-86 and PP2 markedly attenuated claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression induced by US-CM.
source: Both SPP-86 and PP2 markedly attenuated claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression induced by GDNF (Figure 2K) and US-CM (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: GDNF significantly increased TEER values in hCMEC/D3 cells mono-culture BBB model.
source: GDNF significantly increased TEER values (Figure 2M, O) and decreased the permeability of fluorescein and FITC-Dex (Figure 2N, P), which were almost abolished by SPP-86 or PP2.
evidence: This is supported by TEER measurements shown in Figure 2M and 2O.

claim: GDNF decreased the permeability of fluorescein and FITC-Dex in hCMEC/D3 cells mono-culture BBB model.
source: GDNF significantly increased TEER values (Figure 2M, O) and decreased the permeability of fluorescein and FITC-Dex (Figure 2N, P), which were almost abolished by SPP-86 or PP2.
evidence: This is supported by permeability measurements shown in Figure 2N and 2P.

claim: SPP-86 or PP2 almost abolished GDNF-induced increases in TEER values and decreases in permeability.
source: GDNF significantly increased TEER values (Figure 2M, O) and decreased the permeability of fluorescein and FITC-Dex (Figure 2N, P), which were almost abolished by SPP-86 or PP2.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2M-P.

claim: Treatment with SPP-86 or PP2 completely reversed the increased TEER values in the triple co-culture BBB model.
source: Furthermore, treatment with SPP-86 or PP2 completely reversed the increased TEER values (Figure 2Q, S) and decreased permeability of fluorescein and FITC-Dex (Figure 2R, T) in the triple co-culture BBB model.
evidence: This is supported by TEER measurements shown in Figure 2Q and 2S.

claim: Treatment with SPP-86 or PP2 completely reversed the decreased permeability of fluorescein and FITC-Dex in the triple co-culture BBB model.
source: Furthermore, treatment with SPP-86 or PP2 completely reversed the increased TEER values (Figure 2Q, S) and decreased permeability of fluorescein and FITC-Dex (Figure 2R, T) in the triple co-culture BBB model.
evidence: This is supported by permeability measurements shown in Figure 2R and 2T.

claim: Neurons upregulate claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression in hCMEC/D3 cells by secreting GDNF.
source: These results indicate that neurons but also astrocytes upregulate claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression in hCMEC/D3 cells by secreting GDNF.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conditioned medium and GDNF experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Astrocytes upregulate claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression in hCMEC/D3 cells by secreting GDNF.
source: These results indicate that neurons but also astrocytes upregulate claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression in hCMEC/D3 cells by secreting GDNF.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conditioned medium and GDNF experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: GDNF induces claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression by activating GDNF–GFRα1–RET signaling.
source: Subsequently, GDNF induces claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression by activating GDNF–GFRα1–RET signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 2K-T.

claim: GDNF exerts its biological activities by activating several signaling pathways, including the PI3K/AKT, MAPK/ERK, MAPK/JNK, and MAPK/p38 pathways.
source: GDNF exerts its biological activities by activating several signaling pathways, including the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT), mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK)/extracellular regulated kinase (ERK), MAPK/c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), and MAPK/ p38 pathways (Fielder et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GDNF signaling supported by citation.

claim: GDNF increased claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression, accompanied by the phosphorylation of AKT and ERK.
source: GDNF increased claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression, accompanied by the phosphorylation of AKT (p-AKT) and ERK (p-ERK).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: GDNF did not stimulate the phosphorylation of JNK and p38.
source: However, it did not stimulate the phosphorylation of JNK and p38.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: SPP-86, LY29002, and U0126 significantly suppressed GDNF-induced claudin-5 and VE-cadherin expression.
